title: Reading what the compiler tells you
summary: Errors and warnings are information, not punishment. Learn to read compiler and linker diagnostics, find the real cause, and fix it.

quiz.question: GCC reports `greet.cpp:6:34: error: expected ';' before '}' token` (Clang: `expected ';' after return statement`). What is the fix?
options: Add a `;` after the closing `}` of the greeting function on line 7.
Add a `;` at the end of the return statement on line 6, after `"!"`.
Add `#include <string>` — the compiler does not know what a string is.
explanations: Function bodies don't end with `;`. The compiler is telling you it reached the `}` while still expecting the end of the *previous* statement.

Right. `6:34` means line 6, column 34 — the end of the return statement. The compiler only realised something was missing when it saw the next token, `}`. With errors like this, always look *just before* the reported position.
The `}` is correct: it closes the function body. The compiler mentions it only because it is the token it found instead of `;`.
`<string>` is already included on line 2. Read the message literally: it expected a `;`.

quiz.question: Now the compiler says `'greting' was not declared in this scope; did you mean 'greeting'?`. What does "not declared" mean here?
options: The function `greeting` is broken and must be rewritten.
`main` cannot call functions defined in the same file.
The compiler has never seen anything named `greting` — it's a typo for `greeting`, which *is* declared above main.
explanations: `greeting` itself compiles fine now. The error is about a *different* name.
Calling functions in the same file is completely normal — as long as they are declared before the call.

Yes. C++ requires every name to be declared before use, and it matches names exactly. The compiler even suggested the fix. Typos, a missing `#include`, a missing `std::`, or using a variable outside the block it was declared in all produce this error.
`#include` brings in headers (files). `greting` is a function name, and a misspelled one.

steps.title: A warning is a bug report
hints: There are two problems on the `for` line: the type of `i`, and the loop condition. Valid indices for 3 elements are 0, 1 and 2.
`for (std::size_t i = 0; i < scores.size(); ++i)` — or skip indices entirely: `for (int score : scores) total += score;`

steps.title: When the compiler is happy but the build still fails

quiz.question: Both `-c` commands succeed, but linking fails with `undefined reference to 'circle_area(double)'`. What is going on?
options: shapes.cpp has a syntax error the compiler missed.
area.h is missing, so the compiler can't find circle_area.
circle_area is *declared* (in area.h) so shapes.cpp compiles, but no object file *defines* it, so the linker has nothing to connect the call to.
explanations: Both files compiled, so there is no syntax error. Notice *which tool* printed the message — `ld`, the linker.
If the header were missing you'd get a compiler error (`No such file or directory`) — and you didn't.

Exactly. A declaration is a promise: "a function with this signature exists somewhere." The compiler trusts it. The linker is the one who must find the actual definition in some object file — and area.o doesn't contain one.
Never `#include` a .cpp file: you'd end up with duplicate definitions as soon as two files did it. Each .cpp is compiled separately and the linker combines them.

steps.title: Keep the promise

expect.equals: Area of a circle with radius 5: 78.54

hints: The definition must match the declaration in area.h exactly: `double circle_area(double radius)`.
Area of a circle is π·r². `<numbers>` gives you `std::numbers::pi` (C++20).
